Novelty: 4
Justification: While the concept of a global framework with local schedules is not entirely new in HR literature, the solution is clearly innovative in several specific aspects. The detailed breakdown of six distinct work models (distinguishing between compressed, reduced-hours, and nine-day fortnights) prevents the common trap of treating "four-day week" as a monolith. Additionally, the inclusion of a "Global Flexible Work Council" with cross-border inconsistency resolution, combined with strict anti-proximity bias training and channel-specific response norms (e.g., distinguishing emergency paging from team chat), elevates this beyond a standard policy into a highly original operational design.

Usefulness: 5
Justification: The solution is ready to implement. It provides a highly practical, step-by-step roadmap covering legal compliance, role classification, client coverage strategies, and a phased pilot program. By explicitly addressing the administrative friction points that usually derail flexible work—such as how to deduct leave for a 10-hour compressed day, how to handle public holidays falling on non-working days, and how to manage workload tracking—the solution removes the guesswork from execution. The inclusion of a concise "Core global policy statement" at the end makes it immediately actionable for HR teams.

Flexibility: 5
Justification: The approach is highly versatile and avoids one-track thinking. It offers a controlled menu of six work patterns, allowing teams and countries to select what fits their legal, operational, and cultural realities. It also accommodates different role types (location-flexible, hybrid, coverage-dependent, site-dependent) rather than applying a blanket rule to all employees. Furthermore, the phased pilot program explicitly tests multiple models simultaneously (including a control group), ensuring the company doesn't lock itself into a single, potentially flawed paradigm.

Elaboration: 5
Justification: The solution is exhaustively detailed. It leaves no major aspect of flexible work design unaddressed. It covers the legal floor, role classification criteria, the step-by-step request process for employees, right-to-disconnect rules, global collaboration time-zone management, client coverage handoffs, pay/leave calculations, and governance structures. The depth of the 15-point framework, complete with specific examples of how to handle on-call emergencies versus routine messages, demonstrates a comprehensive mastery of the problem space.

Cultural Sensitivity: 5
Justification: The solution is universally appropriate and tackles the core cultural friction points mentioned in the prompt head-on. It explicitly warns against relying on "broad cultural stereotypes" and instead advocates for local employee research (surveys, focus groups) to uncover actual concerns about visibility and loyalty. It protects employees in markets where presenteeism is the norm by explicitly banning "face time" as a performance proxy and requiring managers to document operational reasons for denying flexibility. By allowing local adaptation (e.g., voluntary collaboration days) while enforcing a global anti-retaliation and anti-bias floor, it perfectly balances local cultural nuance with global equity.
